title: Investors who believe in a free lunch are about to get a very expensive bill
text:
Published: Feb 21, 2018 10:11 a.m. ET Share 
The days of easy gains are over, which is why it’s time to diversify into non-correlated investments Courtesy Everett Collection No more wafer thin mints for investors. 
By Analyst 
More and more investors believe there is a free lunch. 
That is, you get something for nothing. In investing, people have been getting a free lunch: Stocks (and bonds) have been rising for years without a bad turnout. 
Will there ever be consequences of massive money printing by central banks, $20 trillion in national debt, a high trade deficit, underfunded social-program liabilities and higher deficits resulting from tax reform? 
One would think so. In theory, gold is supposed to be a hedge against the supposed free lunch investors are enjoying. In practice, it has not worked out that way so far. The key words here are “so far.” Now the free-lunch believers are losing interest in gold. Are they right? Are there other ways to protect oneself? 
Before discussing what to do now, let us explore with a long-term chart of gold. 
Chart 
Please click here for a long-term chart of gold. The chart is of gold ETF GLD, -0.16% Similar observations can be drawn from silver ETF SLV, +0.97% and gold miner ETFs GDX, +1.17% and GDXJ, +1.57% Please note the following from the chart. 
• Gold appears to be forming a bottom. 
• The bottoming process is occurring in a wide range. 
• Significant resistance is ahead. 
• The bottoming process is a weak one; a breakdown from this level cannot be ruled out. 
• For the bottoming process to be complete and gold to take the next up leg, gold will have to decisively break out of the upper resistance line shown on the chart. 
• The chart shows, with a green box, when The Arora Report calls were to buy gold and a red box when The Arora Report calls were to sell gold. 
• The chart also shows The Arora Report calls to back up the truck and buy gold in the $600 an ounce range. The chart also shows The Arora Report call to sell one-half of one’s stake in gold at $1,904, which turned out to be the high, and set a stop loss on the remaining holding at $1,757. Then The Arora Report generated huge profits from gold falling by going short, betting on a decline, as shown on the chart.

Fundamentals 
Here are the three major factors to consider. 
• Gold does not pay any interest. For this reason, rising interest rates are bad for gold. Interest rates are rising now. 
• Gold is priced in dollars. For this reason, gold moves up when the dollar is weak and moves down when the dollar is strong. 
• There are early indications that inflation is picking up. In the very long term, inflation is good for gold. 
Diversification 
Over the past few years, the concept of proper diversification has been lost on many investors. Many investors have become overly concentrated in FAANG stocks (Facebook FB, +2.87% Apple AAPL, +1.21% Amazon AMZN, +1.97% Netflix NFLX, +2.32% and Google GOOG, +2.63% GOOGL, +2.80% In response to my calls for diversification, I often hear from investors that, to diversify, they have added stocks such as Nvidia NVDA, -0.85% Micron Technology MU, +0.87% AMD AMD, -0.50% Applied Materials AMAT, +0.11% and Tesla TSLA, +1.10% to their portfolios. This is not proper diversification, as all of those stocks are going to move together to the downside when the market falls. 
Here is a good test to see if you are diversified. If everything in your portfolio is doing well, you are not diversified. 
A key concept in diversification that many investors miss is having non-correlated assets. Gold is potentially such an asset. It is not correlated to popular ETFs such as S&P 500 ETF SPY, +0.82% Nasdaq 100 ETF QQQ, +1.10% and small-cap ETF IWM, +1.32% as well as to a large number of mutual funds and other similar ETFs. 
Gold ratings 
The Arora Report precious metal ratings are used by bullion dealers, jewelers and investors across the world. 
Here are our current ratings that take into account not only the rewards but also the risks. The goal of every investor ought to be to generate high-risk adjusted returns, i.e., returns in excess of those commensurate with the risk taken. These ratings are designed to produce higher risk-adjusted returns. In our over 30 years in the markets, one of the biggest and most common mistakes we have seen investors make is to ignore risk. 
Gold is: 
• Neutral in the very, very short term. 
• Neutral in the very short term. 
• Mildly positive in the short term. 
• Mildly positive in the medium term. 
• Mildly positive in the long term. 
• Positive in the very long term.

Allocation to precious metals 
For those who are inclined to always have gold in their portfolio, a long allocation of 4%-6% to precious metals from a very long-term perspective at this time is appropriate. This allocation changes with market conditions. 
For diversification reasons, our rules limit maximum allocations to precious metals and miners to 20% of the portfolio. Long-time subscribers to The Arora Report have handsomely profited from our prior allocations of up to 20% of portfolio to precious metals both from long and short sides. 
In addition, we provide money flows in gold by the following categories: smart money, momo (momentum) crowd and short squeeze. We also provide probabilities of reaching various price levels. 
What to do now 
Investors who are holding large stock and bond portfolios ought to consider defensive measures. For the very long term, gold is a good hedge. However, in a short-term correction, gold may not act as a good hedge. Investors may also consider selecting emerging markets such as India, China, Vietnam Russia and South Africa.
